name: Chunking
description: Grouping related pieces of information into meaningful units so people can scan, hold, and work with them more easily. In interface design, chunking turns an undifferentiated wall of options or content into manageable parts.
design_relevance_note: Used in form design, settings, dashboards, and content architecture to break information into sections with clearer hierarchy and less memory burden.
myth_risk_note: Chunking is widely taught as a fundamental memory-organization principle; real backing exists in the corpus, but the specific numeric claims (whether the limit is 'seven' or 'three to five' chunks) are more contested than the popular framing usually acknowledges.
prevalence_note: Dedicated Laws of UX entry and routine NN/g-style content-structure guidance, especially in IA, forms, and content-heavy product work, but less often treated as a standalone flagship law than Fitts/Hick/Miller.

findings.description: Human short-term/working memory reliably holds approximately 7 (plus or minus 2) discrete chunks of information at once — a foundational estimate of working-memory capacity, though the specific figure has since been contested and refined by later research.
findings.source_title: The magical number seven, plus or minus two: Some limits on our capacity for processing information

applications.title: ApartmentGuide.com's unchunked homepage text reads as 'busy, wordy, unwelcoming'
applications.description: NN/g usability testing found that ApartmentGuide.com's homepage presented a 'wall of text' with long lines, no highlighting, and no subheadings. A test participant described it in exactly those terms -- 'busy,' 'wordy,' and 'unwelcoming' -- and said she wasn't interested in reading it, illustrating what happens when content isn't broken into chunks that support scanning.
applications.ethical_note: This is a straightforward content-formatting usability failure, not a persuasion technique -- poor chunking makes content harder to read for everyone involved, with no competing interest between the business and the user that would make this a manipulation question.

applications.title: BBC's short paragraphs and subheadings make an article feel 'nicely split up'
applications.description: In contrast to ApartmentGuide.com's wall of text, NN/g cites a BBC article using short paragraphs, ample white space, subheadings, and a short summary as a positive chunking example. A usability-test participant said she felt it was 'very nicely split up' and could tell at a glance what topics the article covered -- and then went on to read the entire article.
applications.ethical_note: Included deliberately alongside the ApartmentGuide.com example as a matched positive/negative pair, so the batch shows chunking's effect in both directions rather than only the failure case. Good chunking here serves comprehension and genuine reading completion, with no competing business interest in the trade-off.
